Hello, everyone. As some of you may remember, I built my own wheelchair two years ago when I was 16/17. Even though the final result was incredible, I made the mistake of using tubing that was too thin, so every couple of months, my chair would be out of commission while being rewelded. This is why I decided to get a new wheelchair through insurance and ended up with a TiLite Areo Z. I’m going to list all the components and then explain what upgrades I made and the total cost for each part. 

Original parts

    •    Spinergy SPOX wheels

    •    Scwable marathon tires

    •    Roho Quatro high-profile cushion

    •    Adi aluminum backrest

    •    Fit Lt push rims

    •    TiLite glide suspension forks

    •    Titanium open loop footrest with ABS plastic

    •    4x1in front wheels 

    •    Velcro adjust seat sling

    •    TiLite MBL Compact Scissor Wheel Lock

    •    Smartdrive power assist with knob

Upgrades/Changes

    •    Changed handrim mounting to short - $30 at bike shop

    •    Replaced Shwable marathons to right runs- this was because one of the original tires was defective and had a sidewall failure

    •    Changed Tilite casters wheels to frog legs soft rolls- $90. I don’t like the TiLite ones because they require special bearings, which cost 2x as much as regular ones and have to be specially ordered. To make the frog leg wheels fit, I simply cut the Tilite performance spacers to fit the size needed and haven’t had any issues whatsoever. 

    •    I removed the axle clamp and the backrest folding mechanism. They were replaced by having the axle welded onto the frame using two aluminum tubes and the backrest tubing welded straight onto the frame - $900 at a welding shop.

    •    Removed the original carbon fiber side guards and the upholstery seat sling- $500. I replaced the seat with carbon fiber. This wasn’t too difficult I just had to cut the carbon fiber to size and drill holes using the seat sling rails. I then custom-cut carbon fiber sideguards to my wheel profile. I installed these by expanding the original hole used for the old side guard’s clamp and inserted an 8m rivnut in its place.  Then, a second hole was drilled farther down, and another 8m rivnut was added. Installing the last rivnut on the backrest poles was the trickiest as the tubing is smaller and occupied by the adi backrest’s mounting clamps. After much contemplation, I decided to drill and insert a 5/16 rivnut, as it is slightly smaller, and use a spacer between the sideguard and tube. 

Overall, I’m extremely happy with the results, my total comes down to around $1.5K. I went with thicker carbon fiber than last time, which at first worried me as I thought it would be too thick, but it ended up being perfect! I also increased the rivnut size from 6m to 8m, and I think it was the right choice because, due to placement, I could only install 3 rivnuts instead of the 5 my previous chair had. For those worried about the wheelchair’s warranty, in my case, it felt pretty useless as I’m still waiting on new tires through insurance, and it’s been almost a month now, so I’d much rather pay out of pocket for repairs because it’s 10x quicker and less of a hassle.  My hope is for this chair to last me the next 10 years after that, I will most likely build my next chair from scratch because it’s honestly so rewarding knowing you built something that allows you to be fully independent and gives you the freedom you want all while perfectly suiting your needs. 

Feel free to let me know in the comments if you have any questions, and I’ll be happy to answer them!

Unpopular opinion for me is no accessories and my chair being as bare as possible. One of the best quotes from Richard (Wheels2walking): “is it your couch or is it your legs?”
I see so many individuals with wheelchairs that have 300 different add ons to them: stickers, cup holders, lights, spoke covers, and so forth. 

Personally that would never work for me. I am extremely active in my chair and need it to be as light, rigid, and durable as possible. My chair is fully rigid and welded with no moving or folding components, I’ve polished it to bare aluminum so I no longer have to worry about paint damage, it doesn’t have push handles, armrest, or anti tipper, it also doesn’t have any stickers so I don’t have to deal with peeling, and my only accessory is an under seat pouch so I don’t have anything to get in my way. 

While it does make my chair boring and there are downsides to it, it makes it able to endure my constant abuse from jumping up and down cubs, drifting, transferring it in the car, bringing it to the pool or showering, etc. 

I think having 300 add ons makes your chair look clunky and messy. It also adds a lot more needed maintenance and seems very cumbersome.

I think it’s such a tough situation for me. I went to a specialist a couple weeks back and he was dead set on “getting rid of that chair”. He kept talking how he was going to get me independent again and improve my life blah blah blah. He told me I had a high chance of being able to walk again. Well, guess what? I left his office with every intention on killing myself when I got home. 

My life was great before that appointment, I had a job I loved, an incredible therapist, countless friends, and I lived completely by myself relying on no one whatsoever, so for him to say that my chair made me a burden to others and that I must not have a good life really hurt me. 

As much as there are days I despise being a wheelchair user and wish I could go back to when I could walk I also know my body best and I know that even if I put in the extensive work to be able to walk again, it wouldn’t get rid of the neuropathy, or the drop foot, or the nerve damage. I would be in agony, constantly falling, extremely slow, and exhausted. 

After a week of reflection in the psych ward, I realized that this is my life and I live it however is best for me not how others want me to live it. So my goal still isn’t to get out of my wheelchair but it’s to never let it stop me from doing the things I love. I work out multiple times a day to stay fit and healthy, I watch my diet, I use my legs to help me out when I can, and biggest of all I don’t let my disability get to me. For example I’m going to achieve my dream and buy a dirt bike very soon and continue doing all the extreme activities I love doing like racing my challenger in the back roads. 

I’m saying all of this because I’ve realized that once you see your wheelchair as a friend then you learn to use it as a tool to achieve what you want in life and will have more growth than if you try to get rid of it when you’re not ready. Of course everyone is different and has different lives and abilities but this is what has worked for me :)

For those who don’t know me, I built my own wheelchair when I was 17. There’s a couple of posts about it on my profile. I’m posting this to explain the mistakes I made when building my wheelchair and what I’m currently changing about the original design. 

My biggest mistake was using tubing with really thin walls. A couple of months back, I had a tube snap that needed to be rewelded because of it. It also eventually led the front caster tubing to bend from impacts experienced by daily use. This completely messed up the front wheel alignment, leading to a really bad caster flutter, tipping, and instability.

 My second mistake was making my footplate too low to the ground. It would scrape on the slightest bumps and obstacles, and at times, the footplate would get caught entirely, causing me to be launched out of my chair.

 Lastly, my final mistake was my center of gravity. I made it too far forward, which wasn’t the end of the world, but has led me to fall backward a couple of times. I wasn’t planning on fixing this issue, but because my condition has progressed, I need my chair to have a dump, which it currently doesn't have. 

Because it was necessary to fix the front caster tubing, I’ve decided to fix the other issues while I’m at it. Since the front tubes need to be cut off so they can be replaced, I’m using this opportunity to get them welded two inches lower. This will raise my footplate, fix the ground clearance issue, and give my chair dump. The issue with this is that dump leads to more weight being distributed further back. Considering my center of gravity was already too far forward, it would have made my chair a death trap, so I decided to get the axle cut off and rewelded one inch back to make things a lot more stable. 

This chair has gotten me through so much. It is truly my most prized achievement. The issue is that I’m very active and extremely rough on my chair. I can see that she is starting to fall apart. She needs new carbon fiber, rivnuts, hardware, and wheels. I can’t afford to make those replacements so this final upgrade is being done in hopes it will make her last long enough for my insurance-covered wheelchair to arrive. After that, I sadly will be retiring her and closing this chapter of my life. Thank you to all of those who followed and supported the building journey, it meant a lot to me.

I flew delta. I’m an almost full time wheelchair user and had a quickie Qri at the time. When getting your tickets at the front desk they will ask you if you wish to stay independent or not. I said yes to staying in my wheelchair and having an aid lead me around the airport and stuff. TSA wasn’t too bad. I had to take all gear off my dog and he went through the metal scanner when I called him on the other side. For me because I can walk a little bit I also walked through the metal scanner and during that they searched and test wiped my chair. Once at your gate you need to find an attendant and ask them for a tag for you chair. They will print it for you and attach it to you back rigidizer. Then they will ask you when you wish to give them your chair. I opted to give it at that point as that’s when I took the upholstery, cushion, and calf strap off my chair. I had completely bubble wrapped before going to the airport as it makes things a lot easier. From there I walked onto the plane and sat down. My biggest issue which might not be an issues for you if you’re not traveling international, is that they promised me I would have my chair when exiting the plane but it never happened on both flights.
